source.title: Learning Locally, Revising Globally: Global Reviser for Federated Learning with Noisy Labels
source.authors: Yu-Xin Tian; Mou-Xing Yang; Yu-Hao Zhou; Jian Wang; Qing Ye; Tong-Liang Liu; Gang Niu; Jian-Cheng Lv

page_placements.theme: Federated training changes memorization and generalization trajectories

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper and appendix; no document problem noted.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures noisy-label memorization over training in federated models and compares it with centralized training, using a different training setting from the claim’s original sources.
record.gate_note: The study tests heterogeneous label-noise settings, not completely random relabeling. Its observation results are mainly in figures; the text summarizes them without numerical values. The FedGR benchmark tables report test accuracy for the proposed method and baselines, so those results do not directly measure whether the claim’s models fit random labels.
record.test_reason: FedGR uses the memorization effect to motivate warm-up and label correction. Its observation experiments compare noisy-label memorization in federated and centralized models, but do not establish that clean patterns are learned before noisy labels. Slower noise memorization across training methods does not itself test V6; no other version is directly tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors report slower noisy-label overfitting by federated global models and use this observation to motivate FedGR. Clean-pattern-first learning and cancellation of client-specific noise updates are proposed explanations; theoretical analysis of the observed phenomenon is left for future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines federated training with heterogeneous client data and label noise, comparing the global model with centralized training; it does not reproduce the original random-label intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: The memorization and test-performance observations are reported across datasets, client sampling ratios, local epochs, noise ratios, client scales, and I.I.D versus Non.I.I.D partitions. The text says the effect persists across these settings, with a qualification at high noise ratios.

fits_no_version.finding: Under moderate label noise, federated global models memorize fewer noisy labels than centralized models throughout training and avoid the reported decline in test performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Federated averaging slows noisy-label memorization relative to centralized training in the tested CIFAR settings.

fits_no_version.finding: At 50% and 80% noise, federated global models still memorize noisy labels more slowly, but may fail to reach centralized training's peak test accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Slower noisy-label memorization in federated training can coexist with lower peak predictive performance.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The observation results are presented primarily in figures, with no numerical values in the text summaries. The authors note that at high noise ratios the global model may not achieve the centralized model’s peak test performance. The study evaluates noisy labels rather than fully random relabeling.
record.rows_left_out: The observation figures report multiple individual configurations for CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, client sampling ratios, local epochs, and client-specific comparisons (Figures 5–17). They are not extracted as separate rows because the supplied text does not give separate numerical values and the text-level summaries aggregate the outcomes. FedGR benchmark tables and ablations are omitted because they report the proposed method’s performance on noisy-label benchmarks, not whether the claim’s random-label behavior occurs.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Time to fit true versus random labels and convergence slowdown as corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit across corruption fractions from zero to one and steadily increasing test error toward chance.
Whether explicit regularization prevents fitting random labels and whether its removal impairs true-label generalization.
Direct measurement of clean-pattern learning before noisy-label memorization. This ordering is invoked as a possible explanation, rather than established by the reported comparison.

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text does not preserve readable curves for Figures 5–11. The authors' statement that both training methods eventually fit all noisy labels occurs within a possible explanation, not a demonstrated zero-training-error result. FedGR accuracy benchmarks and augmentation ablations do not establish any listed version.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test completely random labeling, training error near zero, chance test error, or whether the original architecture and training hyperparameters are unchanged.
Does not measure training time to fit true versus random labels or convergence time across corruption fractions.
Does not train on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Studies noisy-label memorization at several noise ratios, but does not report perfect training fit across the full corruption range or test error rising steadily toward chance.
Does not test whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation prevent fitting random labels, or whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
Does not directly compare learning shared real-label patterns with learning random labels; its observations concern noisy-label memorization in federated versus centralized training.

rows.subject: global model of FL
rows.operation_detail: Measured the percentage of noisy labels memorized during training.

conditions.value: moderate noisy ratio; specific observation settings shown in Figures 5–10

rows.measure: Percentage of noisy labels memorized over training
rows.baseline: centralized trained model; exact values figure only
rows.value: The text says the global model memorizes less noisy labels throughout training than centralized training; exact values figure only.
rows.note: The text summarizes results across the plotted settings but does not give numerical values. This measures slower memorization of noisy labels, not fitting completely random labels.
rows.check: The reported difference between federated and centralized noisy-label memorization does not measure the clean-before-noise ordering required by V6. Lower memorization is not a partial V6 effect. The observation stage is vanilla training for 200 centralized epochs or FL rounds. Tables 10–11 specify 10 clients, local epochs 1 or 10, and overall noise ratios 18.66% or 15.36%. Figure 1 also supplies a textual bound: the CIFAR-10 global model memorizes at most 30% of noisy labels.

rows.subject: global model of FL
rows.operation_detail: Measured noisy-label memorization and test performance during training at high noise ratios.
rows.measure: Noisy labels memorized and test performance over training
rows.baseline: centralized trained model; exact values figure only
rows.value: The text says the global model memorizes noisy labels more slowly and does not suffer a drop in test performance; it may not achieve the centralized model’s peak test performance.
rows.note: The description qualifies the comparison: at high noise, test performance does not drop, but the global model may not reach centralized training’s peak.
rows.check: Slower noisy-label memorization and preserved test performance relative to centralized training do not establish when clean patterns are learned relative to noisy labels. Table 13 specifies client sampling ratio 0.2 and one local epoch. The observation stage is vanilla training for 200 centralized epochs or FL rounds.

relation.reason: The method relies on the memorization effect; slower noise memorization in federated training does not establish any listed claim version.

tranche.reason: FedGR uses the memorization effect for warm-up and label correction. Its observations compare noisy-label memorization across training methods without testing clean-pattern-first learning.

source_check.notes: Tables 12–13 specify ResNet18, 20/100 clients, sampling ratio 0.2 and one local epoch for the high-noise observations. Clean-pattern-first learning and cancellation of noise updates are proposed explanations, not established temporal results; exact performance values are figure-only.
